name: Muyu, Kawip/Kawiyet dialect
catalog_citation: Zahrer, Alexander. 2023. A grammar of Muyu: A Lowland Ok language of Western New Guinea. PhD dissertation, Universität Münster (repositorium.uni-muenster.de).

catalog_quote: Evidence for lexical stress in Muyu varies. Both Drabbe (1954) and Christensen (2013) report the existence of non-phonemic accent/stress on the lexeme level for their respective dialect. According to Drabbe, an “accent” (which is not further specified) is on the last syllable of each word, and a “minor accent” (i.e. secondary stress) on the first syllable of a trisyllabic word. In contrast, Christensen reports the lexical stress ... always to be on the first syllable. ... However, our findings for the Kawip dialect point in another direction. It seems that speakers of Kawip do not assign lexical stress at all. Although we did not investigate the topic systematically, there are two kinds of (very preliminary) evidence for a lack of lexical stress. sources.citation: Zahrer, Alexander. 2025. Children of the sago: Muyu texts (Open Text Collections 3). Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.15781820. 330 pp (PDF).
sources.quote: 'Unlike other languages of the Ok family, Muyu does not have lexical tone. Furthermore, there seems to be no lexical stress. Prosodic features take place in larger units, e.g. falling and rising intonation to signal finality or continuation in complex sentences (see Zahrer 2024).'

sources.citation: Zahrer, Alexander. 2024. Exploring natural speech intonation of an under-researched Papuan language. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2024 (Leiden), 1095-1099. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2024-221.
sources.quote: Intonation study only (contour clustering of 325 IU-final f0 contours: final verbs -> falling, medial/multi verbs -> rising/level boundary tones). On word prosody it says only that 'language-specific phonological categories (e.g. pitch accents) have not been established yet'; no claim about lexical stress.
